newsitem.title: USA: Clinton off to Australia, Asia after space drama.
newsitem.headline: Clinton off to Australia, Asia after space drama.

text.p: President Bill Clinton begins a nine-day trip to Australia and Asia on Monday that for awhile seemed likely to be overshadowed by the fall to earth of a crippled Russian Mars space probe.

The U.S. Space Command said late on Sunday the disabled six-tonne probe was believed to have reentered the atmosphere over the Pacific Ocean west of Chile just after 8:30 p.m. EST (0130 Monday GMT) and that if any part of it survived, it had fallen harmlessly into the sea.

The spacecraft, with four tiny batteries powered by lethal plutonium, lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday but failed to break out of Earth's orbit after a booster rocket misfired.

Earlier on Sunday, it had appeared that it would crash to earth north of the Australian capital of Canberra, triggering telephone consultations between Clinton and Prime Minister John Howard that interrupted the president's rain-soaked Hawaiiian golfing weekend.
Although the crisis passed, the issue of raining space junk is likely to wind up on the agenda of Clinton's talks with Howard and figure in his speech to the Australian Parliament on Wednesday.

Clinton, on his first foreign trip since his re-election, also planned to tour the Great Barrier Reef and hit the links with Australian golf pro Greg Norman before going on to the Philippines for the annual Asian trade summit next weekend.

At a Hawaiian luau -- a Polynesian-style barbeque -- hosted by Gov. Ben Cayetano on Saturday night, Clinton said the purpose of his trip was to promote a new century of peace and prosperity in the Pacific region, which has been a cauldron of war for much of the 20th century.
On the fringes of the summit, Clinton will hold important bilateral talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.

It will be Clinton's fourth meeting with his Chinese counterpart, and it comes amid strained relations between Washington and Beijing because of U.S. displeasure with China's policy on trade, Taiwan and human rights.

"The two presidents will have a broad agenda that will include regional security issues, such as the Korean peninsula, preventing an arms race in Southeast Asia, (nuclear) non- proliferation, trade and human rights," Deputy National Security Adviser Samuel Berger told reporters.

The APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit will inevitably be a reminder of how the president's Democratic Party cultivated wealthy Asians as it raised the tens of millions of dollars needed for the Nov. 5 election campaign.

On the eve of his Pacific trip, Clinton told the New York Times that he had twice discussed policy about Indonesia and China with James Riady, an Indonesian banker at the centre of inquiries into the campaign funding controversy. But he said Riady, a longtime friend who met him at the APEC summit in Jakarta two years ago, had never influenced policy decisions.

Clinton also said it had been a mistake for the Democratic National Committee to send John Huang, a former employee of Riady, to Taiwan to raise money for the 1996 campaign. Huang's trip occurred two months after Clinton sent warships to protect Taiwan from Chinese military harassment.
Clinton will wind up his trip with a visit to Thailand, which will have just finished completed parliamentary elections.
Berger said that part of the trip was intended to provide "further proof ... that democracy is expanding in Asia just as it is elsewhere around the world."

The United States has a long history of military cooperation with Bangkok and works with Thai authorities to control the flow of drugs from the opium fields in the Golden Triangle, which includes parts of Thailand, Burma and Laos.
Clinton is due back in Washington on Nov. 27, the day before the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.
